assets.topic: Blind Obedience to Authority: Milgram's Shock Paradigm
assets.visual_frame_description: The player sits at the 'teacher' desk in a Yale laboratory in Linsly-Chittenden Hall, facing a shock generator with thirty switches rising from 15 volts to an ominous XXX at 435 and 450 volts. A gray-coated experimenter stands nearby giving scripted instructions. Through the intercom, a mild-mannered middle-aged learner in the next room begins making errors and complaining that the shocks are starting to hurt.
assets.player_mission: Play the role of the teacher and decide at each protest whether to continue pressing the next-higher voltage switch or to end your participation. Recognize the authority prods for what they are and determine the point at which you must stop.
key_concepts: In Milgram's obedience paradigm, two of every three volunteers (65 percent) delivered the maximum 450-volt shock to the learner-victim.
The shock generator used thirty switches increasing by 15 volts, from a mild initial shock up to switches labeled only with an ominous XXX.
Forty psychiatrists predicted that less than 1 percent of Americans would go all the way to the end, expecting only sadists to do so, and most predicted dropouts at the 150-volt level.
The experimenter's role was played by a high school biology teacher whose authority came from being perceived as a representative of a legitimate scientific system.
Most participants dissented verbally, saying they did not want to continue, yet still complied behaviorally when the experimenter insisted they had no choice.
Starting with a mild 15-volt shock and increasing in gradual 15-volt steps made each new level seem only slightly different from the prior action.
The experimenter claimed he would take responsibility for anything that happened to the learner, a tactic that diffused the teacher's sense of accountability.
The 450-volt maximum became the 'easy way out' because finishing the panel offered escape without directly confronting the authority figure.
Compliance rates could soar to over 90 percent when the subject was part of a 'teaching team' or fall to less than 10 percent when peers rebelled.
When the learner fell silent at 330 volts, almost everyone who had gotten that far continued to the bitter end rather than quitting.
Milgram's research was motivated by his deep concern about how readily the Nazis had obediently killed Jews during the Holocaust.
A Bridgeport, Connecticut, replication in a run-down office building away from Yale still produced high obedience, showing the effect was not due to Yale's prestige.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests blind obedience to authority: ordinary people will inflict serious harm when a legitimate-appearing authority insists they continue. Milgram showed that 65 percent of volunteers went all the way to 450 volts, and that compliance could swing from over 90 percent to under 10 percent depending on the situational variables.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the psychology of blind obedience: the willingness of ordinary citizens to obey an authority figure whose demands conflict with their own moral standards. The key insight is that verbal dissent does not equal behavioral disobedience, and that the situation's structure, not personal disposition, determines who obeys.
assets.stage_1_observation: You press the 150-volt switch, labeled 'Strong Shock,' and the learner begins complaining that his heart is bothering him and that he wants to be let out. The experimenter tells you that you have no choice but to continue.
assets.stage_1_question: The learner says his heart condition is bothering him and demands to be released. The experimenter insists you continue. What should you recognize about your own position right now?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: You should recognize that you are free to leave at any time, since nothing physically prevents you from walking out, and that the experimenter's insistence that you have no choice is a situational pressure you can resist. Continuing despite the learner's heart complaint is the first major step on the obedience path.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You have just pressed the 330-volt switch and the learner has gone completely silent, possibly unconscious. The experimenter orders you to treat the silence as a wrong answer and continue to the next level.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Refuse to continue and end your participation immediately, because continuing past silence means you are no longer responding to the learner's pain but only to the authority's demand. Almost everyone who reached this point continued to the end, making this the critical moment to break the obedience chain.

assets.topic: Conformity to a Unanimous Majority: Asch's Line Studies
assets.visual_frame_description: The player is participant number eight in Asch's line-judgment study, seated beside seven peers who are actually confederates. A card shows three lines of differing lengths and a comparison line on another card; the task appears trivially easy. On a critical trial, each of the seven peers in turn reports that the obviously wrong line matches the comparison line, then all look expectantly at the player.
assets.player_mission: Complete the perceptual judgment task while a unanimous majority reports answers that contradict what you clearly see. Decide whether to trust your own perception or go along with the group on the twelve critical trials, and recognize the mechanisms that pressure you to conform.
key_concepts: Asch's conformity research showed that subjects yielded to an incorrect unanimous majority about 70 percent of the time on some critical trials.
Thirty percent of the original subjects conformed on the majority of trials, and only a quarter maintained their independence throughout the testing.
Without group pressure, subjects made errors less than 1 percent of the time on the line-length task.
Some conformers were aware they were going along because it was easier, while others resolved the conflict by actually believing the group was right.
All those who yielded underestimated how much they had conformed, recalling much less yielding than had actually occurred.
With just one person giving an incorrect judgment, a participant exhibited uneasiness but maintained independence.
With a majority of three people opposed, errors rose to 32 percent.
Giving the subject a partner whose views agreed with his greatly diminished the power of the majority and cut errors to one fourth of the prior level.
The resistance gained from a partner endured even after the partner left the room.
Conformity arises from informational needs, using others' views to navigate the world, and normative needs, seeking acceptance by agreeing with others.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests conformity to a unanimous majority: when a group unanimously reports something that contradicts clear perception, most individuals yield rather than maintain independence. Asch found that peer support was the single most powerful way to restore independence, cutting conformity errors to one fourth.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests conformity pressure: the tendency to yield to a unanimous majority even when the correct answer is obvious. The critical lesson is that conformity is driven both by informational needs (assuming the group knows more) and normative needs (wanting to be accepted), and that a single ally can break the majority's power.
assets.stage_1_observation: On the first critical trial, all seven peers have reported that the long line matches the comparison line when you clearly see that the medium line is the match. All heads turn to you for your answer, and the room is expectantly quiet.
assets.stage_1_question: Facing a unanimous majority that contradicts your clear perception, what should you trust, and what will happen to your judgment if you go along?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: You should trust your own clear perception and state it independently, while recognizing that most people would yield under this pressure. Going along would be driven by normative pressure to be accepted and informational doubt, and you would likely underestimate afterward how much you had conformed.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The experimenter reassigns the seating so that another participant who sees the same line as you answers before you do, providing a partner in dissent. You now face the same unanimous majority on the next critical trial.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Use the partner's agreement to maintain your independence, because a single partner whose views are in line with yours greatly diminishes the majority's power and reduces conformity errors to one fourth, with the resistance effect enduring even after the partner leaves.

assets.topic: The Lure of the Inner Ring: Initiation Into Privileged Groups
assets.visual_frame_description: A senior engineer, Marco, invites the player, a junior product manager named Priya, to an after-work drink at a neighborhood bar. Over coffee and small talk, Marco leans in with a confidential smile and hints that the 'we' on his team always takes a shortcut that is not quite in line with the official rules, something 'the public would never understand.' He makes clear the invitation is a test of whether Priya belongs.
assets.player_mission: Recognize the seductive pull of C. S. Lewis's Inner Ring and decide how to respond when an insider offers privileged access in exchange for a small bending of the rules. Identify the psychological mechanism at work and choose the response that keeps you out of the scoundrel's path.
key_concepts: C. S. Lewis argued that the passion for the Inner Ring is most skillful in making a man who is not yet a very bad man do very bad things.
The quest for the Inner Ring is nurtured from within: there is no peer-pressure power without self-pressure for them to want you.
The lure of the Inner Ring is the desire to be 'in' and not 'out,' with the terror of being left outside as its motivating force.
The fear of rejection when one wants acceptance can cripple initiative and negate personal autonomy.
Authorities can command total obedience not through punishments or rewards but through the lure of acceptance coupled with the threat of rejection.
Even strangers gain power when they promise us a special place at their table of shared secrets, 'just between you and me.'
Lewis described the subtle initiation into a private Inner Ring that can turn good people into 'scoundrels' through escalating small compromises.
The hint of wrongdoing comes disguised as a triviality, sandwiched between jokes, at the moment you are most anxious not to appear crude, naive, or a prig.
People are drawn into the Inner Ring not by desire for gain or ease but because they cannot bear to be thrust back into the cold outer world.
The escalation is gradual: this week something a little further from the rules, next year something further still, all in the jolliest, friendliest spirit.
A forty-year-old woman pleaded guilty to providing sex, drugs, and alcohol to high school boys because she wanted to be a 'cool mom' and finally feel like one of the group.
Being cast into the out-group is so terrifying that some people will do virtually anything to avoid it.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the lure of the Inner Ring: the desire to be accepted by a privileged in-group, which motivates people to take the first small, rule-bending step that begins a slide into wrongdoing. Zimbardo argues this basic motive for belonging, when perverted by those with power to admit or deny access, transforms good people into scoundrels through gradual escalation.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the psychology of the Inner Ring, C. S. Lewis's concept that the centripetal pull of acceptance into a privileged group is a powerful force pushing people across the boundary between good and evil. The mechanism combines the lure of acceptance with the terror of rejection, and its power grows through gradual, friendly escalation.
assets.stage_1_observation: Marco confides that the senior team 'always does it this way,' a shortcut that bends a fairness rule but that 'no one outside would understand.' He is watching to see whether Priya is worthy of the inner circle. He insists the matter stays 'just between you and me.'
assets.stage_1_question: At this first, seemingly trivial invitation to bend a rule as a member of the 'we,' what psychological force is pulling Priya toward acceptance, and what is the safest response?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The force is the lure of acceptance into the Inner Ring combined with the terror of rejection, not any desire for personal gain. The safest response is to decline the insider shortcut without humiliating Marco, because agreeing to the first small compromise is the entry step onto a slippery path that escalates to scoundrelism.
assets.stage_2_intervention: A few weeks later, Priya is now a trusted insider. Marco proposes something a little further from the rules, framed as a favor only insiders can do, again in the most friendly and confidential spirit. He reminds her of what they share and of the secret they already keep.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Priya must recognize the escalating pattern Lewis described and firmly refuse to take the next step further from the rules, because each successive compromise comes in the jolliest, friendliest spirit and leads further down the path. Breaking the pattern now, while the stakes are still small, is the only way to avoid becoming a scoundrel.

assets.topic: Administrative Obedience: The Hostile Interview Paradigm
assets.visual_frame_description: The player is a research participant at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, seated at a desk with a microphone to a neighboring room. On the other side of the wall, a job applicant waits to take a selection test. The experimenter instructs the player, acting as 'administrator,' to deliver fifteen graded stress remarks that denigrate the applicant's performance and personality, continuing despite any protests, so that the applicant fails the test and stays unemployed.
assets.player_mission: Decide whether to comply with an authority's demand to administer fifteen hostile stress remarks that will sabotage a job applicant's chances. Recognize the cover story that justifies the harm and choose whether to obey, dissenting only verbally, or to actually stop the harm.
key_concepts: In the Dutch administrative obedience paradigm, 91 percent of subjects obeyed the authoritative experimenter to the very end of the line.
When the same dilemma was presented hypothetically, more than 90 percent of comparable respondents said they would not comply.
The task required fifteen graded stress remarks that were critical of the applicant's performance and denigrated his personality, such as 'That was really stupid of you.'
The remarks placed the applicant under such intense psychological strain that he did not perform satisfactorily and consequently failed to get the job.
Dissent by participant-administrators was countered with up to four prods by the experimenter before they were permitted to stop.
The subjects were told the ability to work under stress was not an essential job requirement, yet the procedure had to be followed to assist the researcher's project.
In the control condition, where subjects could stop at any point, no one fully obeyed.
The same high obedience held even when personnel officers served as subjects despite their professional code of ethics.
High obedience was also found when subjects received advance information weeks before the study and had time to reflect on their hostile role.
Obedience could be reduced by having several peers rebel before the subject's turn or by notifying the subject of legal liability if the applicant were harmed and sued.
The paradigm involved twenty-five separate studies with nearly 500 participants conducted at Utrecht University between 1982 and 1985.
Modern authority violence is often mediated and administrative rather than physical, with consequences that are not directly observable.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests administrative obedience: ordinary people will perform psychologically harmful acts against an innocent victim when instructed by an authority, even when the act serves no legitimate purpose beyond the researcher's data collection. Zimbardo notes that 91 percent of participants delivered all fifteen hostile remarks, while none fully obeyed in the control condition where the authority pressure was removed.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests administrative obedience, the modern extension of Milgram's findings in which authorities inflict harm through mediated, nonphysical means. The central trap is that verbal dissent feels like resistance while behavioral compliance continues, and the authority's cover story provides a justification that makes continued harm feel acceptable.
assets.stage_1_observation: You deliver the fifth remark, 'That was really stupid of you,' and hear the applicant's voice waver through the wall as his test performance deteriorates. You dissent, saying you do not want to continue, and the experimenter prods you: 'You must continue; it is necessary for the research.'
assets.stage_1_question: The applicant is clearly distressed and failing the test because of your remarks, and you have voiced your objection. The experimenter prods you to continue. What should you recognize about your dissent and your situation?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: You should recognize that your verbal dissent alone does not change the outcome, since the harm comes from your continued compliance, and that stopping the remarks is the only effective resistance. Because nothing but the authority's prodding prevents you from stopping, ending the procedure now is the decisive act.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The experimenter tells you the research is studying how stress affects test performance and insists that finishing all fifteen remarks is required for the data. You now realize the applicant's stress tolerance is not an essential job requirement and the harm serves no purpose beyond collecting data.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Refuse and stop the procedure, because when the authority pressure is removed or the cover story collapses, full obedience disappears, as the control condition showed. Continuing to deliver remarks that cost an innocent applicant his job, with no legitimate justification, is administrative obedience to an unjust demand.

assets.topic: The Banality of Evil: Eichmann's Ordinary Evil
assets.visual_frame_description: The player sits in a courtroom in Jerusalem in 1961, observing Adolf Eichmann, a middle-aged man in a glass booth who appears entirely ordinary, neatly dressed and composed. He speaks in bureaucratic language about his role arranging the transport of millions to their deaths, insisting he was only following orders. Half a dozen psychiatrists had certified him as normal.
assets.player_mission: Act as a juror evaluating Eichmann's defense and decide what his psychological normality and obedience-to-orders defense mean for his responsibility. Distinguish the banality of evil from the portrait of a sadistic monster, and render a judgment on the moral meaning of his actions.
key_concepts: Hannah Arendt's 1963 classic Eichmann in Jerusalem coined the phrase 'the banality of evil.'
Eichmann's defense was 'I was only following orders,' the same testimony given by other Nazi leaders.
Half a dozen psychiatrists certified Eichmann as normal, with one remarking he was 'more normal than I am after having examined him.'
Arendt concluded that Eichmann was neither perverted nor sadistic but 'terribly and terrifyingly normal.'
Arendt argued that this new type of criminal commits his crimes under circumstances that make it well-nigh impossible for him to know or feel that he is doing wrong.
Arendt's analysis was the first to deny the dispositional view that evil resides in the personal makeup of evildoers.
Zimbardo argues the banality of evil applies to the 'ordinary British lads' of the London bombings and the 'mundane people' of the 9/11 plotters.
Andrew Silke observed that the most terrifying thing about suicide bombers is their sheer normality, with no traces of alcohol or drugs in forensic examinations.
The perpetrator of the strip-search scam was a former corrections officer, and similar hoaxes were carried out in 68 fast-food settings in 32 states.
Columbine-style reactions typically report 'He was such a good kid' because observers misjudge how situationally influenced behavior can be.
Zimbardo argues that deindividuation makes the perpetrator anonymous, reducing personal accountability and self-monitoring.
Dehumanization takes away the humanity of potential victims, rendering them animallike or as nothing.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the banality of evil, Arendt's claim that horrific crimes can be committed by entirely ordinary, unremarkable people who do not feel they are doing wrong. Zimbardo uses this concept to argue that situational and systemic forces, not sadistic dispositions, explain how normal people become executioners.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the banality of evil: the idea that evil is often committed by ordinary, even admirable people rather than by monsters, because situations make it difficult for them to recognize wrongdoing. The enemy is the comfortable assumption that evildoers are pathological and different from us.
assets.stage_1_observation: Eichmann speaks calmly, using administrative language about schedules, transport, and paperwork for the millions shipped to their deaths. Psychiatrists have declared him perfectly normal, and he shows no sadistic pleasure, no rage, and no apparent awareness of wrongdoing.
assets.stage_1_question: Given Eichmann's utter normality and his lack of malice, how should his mental state be understood in relation to the crimes?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: His normality should not be read as innocence; rather, it illustrates the banality of evil, in which crimes are committed under circumstances that make it nearly impossible for the actor to feel he is doing wrong. The absence of sadistic pathology makes the case more terrifying, not less.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The defense argues that because Eichmann was a small cog following lawful orders of his superiors, he cannot be held personally responsible for the murders. The court must decide how to weigh his obedience against his individual responsibility.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Reject the obedience defense as a removal of personal responsibility, because Zimbardo's analysis holds that asserting one's personal authority and taking full responsibility for one's actions is the way to avoid crimes of obedience. Following orders does not absolve the individual who arranged the deaths of millions.

assets.topic: The Double-Dose Order: Physician Power Over Nurses
assets.visual_frame_description: The player is an auditor reviewing hospital records of a phone call received by Nurse Marta Ivanova on a busy med-surg floor. The screen shows the medication label for 'Astrogen,' which indicates that 5 milliliters is the usual dose and warns that 10 milliliters is the maximum, alongside a call log showing an order for 20 milligrams. The player must diagnose why a competent nurse began to comply with the unauthorized order.
assets.player_mission: Analyze the timed observation log, the nurse's baseline behavior, and the phone-call transcript to determine why the nurse nearly administered a double-maximum dose. Deliver the correct diagnosis of the psychological mechanism and rule out the distractors.
key_concepts: In a real hospital test, twenty-two nurses individually received a phone order from an unknown staff doctor to administer 20 milligrams of 'Astrogen' to a patient.
The Astrogen label stated that 5 milliliters was the usual dose and warned that 10 milliliters was the maximum dose, so the order doubled the maximum.
When the dilemma was presented hypothetically to a dozen nurses, ten said they would refuse to obey the order.
When actually put on the hot seat, all but one of the twenty-two nurses started to pour the medication before researchers stopped them.
A survey of a large sample of registered nurses found that nearly half (46 percent) recalled carrying out a physician's order they felt could have had harmful consequences.
Nurses who complied attributed less responsibility to themselves than to the physician.
The nurses identified the primary basis of physicians' social power as 'legitimate power,' the right to provide overall care to the patient.
Thousands of hospitalized patients die needlessly each year due to staff mistakes, some involving unquestioning obedience to wrong orders.
The solitary disobedient nurse, in Zimbardo's words, should have been given a raise and a hero's medal.
Authority influence is typically direct and without subtlety: 'You do what I tell you to do.'
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests obedience to legitimate authority in the medical hierarchy: nurses who would refuse a harmful order in the abstract nonetheless comply when a physician issues it directly. Zimbardo shows that the physician's 'legitimate power' leads compliant nurses to attribute responsibility away from themselves.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Why did 21 of 22 experienced nurses begin to pour a medication at double the labeled maximum dose based solely on a phone order from a doctor they had never met?
assets.subject_baseline: Marta Ivanova is a 34-year-old registered nurse with 11 years on a medical-surgical unit. She is known as meticulous: she double-checks labels, questions unclear orders, and once refused to give a medication she believed was miscounted, calling the pharmacy to verify the dose before administering anything.
observed_nonverbal_log: 09:02 Call comes in; Marta picks up, reads the unit's protocol book while listening.
09:03 Marta's brows knit; she holds the phone to her shoulder and turns the Astrogen vial to read the label twice.
09:04 She asks the caller to repeat the dosage and the patient name; her voice drops and she glances at the charge nurse's desk.
09:05 Marta sets the label back on the cart and reaches for a syringe, hesitating with her hand on the vial cap.
09:06 She begins drawing up the medication, hands slightly unsteady, without having hung up the phone.
09:07 The researcher intervenes and stops her before any medication reaches the patient.
interrogation_transcript: Doctor (phone): 'This is Dr. Moreau in the cardiology clinic. Administer 20 milligrams of Astrogen to Room 412 now, so it takes effect before I arrive. I will sign the order then.'
Marta: 'Twenty milligrams? Doctor, the label here shows the maximum is ten.'
Doctor: 'I am aware of the label. This is my patient, and I am ordering twenty milligrams immediately. Are you refusing?'
Marta: 'No, Doctor, I am just confirming. I will get the patient ready.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Blind obedience to the physician's legitimate power, in which the nurse construed the unauthorized order as legitimate and attributed responsibility for the harmful consequence to the physician rather than to herself.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Marta's baseline shows she verifies doses and questions unclear orders, so carelessness is not the explanation. The timed log shows her reading the label twice, confirming she knew the dose doubled the maximum. Her hesitations reveal an internal conflict, yet when the 'legitimate' authority insisted and asked if she was refusing, she complied, exactly as the research found: nurses submitted because the doctor's power was seen as legitimate and responsibility was attributed to the physician. The single disobedient nurse in the study demonstrates the behavior was avoidable and a genuine act of resistance.
distractors: Marta was afraid the doctor would physically harm her or her patient.
Marta misread the label and genuinely believed 20 milligrams was within the safe range.
Marta was a poorly trained or negligent nurse who routinely ignored dosing standards.

assets.topic: Authority in Absentia: The Strip-Search Phone Scam
assets.visual_frame_description: The player is an investigator reviewing surveillance footage and an audio transcript from the back room of a fast-food restaurant. An assistant manager, Kevin Marsh, is on the phone with a man who identifies himself as Police Officer Scott, while a frightened eighteen-year-old employee stands in the rear room. The footage shows Kevin nodding, saying 'Yes, sir,' and complying with a series of escalating instructions from the unseen caller.
assets.player_mission: Analyze the observation log and call transcript to diagnose why an assistant manager strip-searched an innocent employee on the word of an anonymous caller. Determine the real mechanism behind this 'authority influence in absentia' and rule out the dispositional explanations.
key_concepts: Strip-search scams were perpetrated in a number of fast-food restaurant chains throughout the United States.
The caller identified himself as a police officer, insisted on being called 'Sir,' and used inside information about store procedures to seem legitimate.
The caller was a former corrections officer, and similar hoaxes were carried out in 68 fast-food settings in 32 states across a half-dozen chains.
The scam victimized both male and female employees and deceived assistant managers of many restaurants.
The con man knew how to solicit information through skillfully guided questions, as stage magicians and mind readers do.
Donna Summers, a McDonald's assistant manager in Mount Washington, Kentucky, was fired for being deceived into participating in the hoax.
Summers observed, 'Unless you're put in that situation, at that time, how do you know what you would do. You don't.'
Ester Reiter concluded that obedience to authority is the most valued trait in fast-food workers, whose assembly-line process deliberately removes thought and discretion.
Retired FBI special agent Dan Jablonski noted the workers are not trained to use common sense but to say 'Can I help you?'
Zimbardo argues the analysis must shift from blaming victims to recognizing the power of situational forces.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests authority influence in absentia: people obey an anonymous voice that merely appears to be a legitimate authority, even when compliance violates store policy and basic morality. Zimbardo argues the scam's success in dozens of locations across 32 states proves situational power, not individual gullibility, is the operative cause.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Why did assistant manager Kevin Marsh order a strip-search of an innocent eighteen-year-old employee based entirely on a phone call from a man who claimed to be a police officer?
assets.subject_baseline: Kevin Marsh is a 29-year-old assistant manager with six years at the chain. Coworkers describe him as by-the-book, deferential to authority, and anxious about being blamed for problems. He has never had a disciplinary write-up and is known for following corporate policy exactly as trained, including the scripted customer greeting 'Can I help you?'
observed_nonverbal_log: 11:12 Kevin answers the phone; his posture stiffens as the caller identifies himself as Officer Scott of the local police.
11:14 Kevin repeats 'Yes, sir' three times in the first two minutes and stands straighter, gripping the phone with both hands.
11:17 He looks at the security camera and then back at the new employee in the rear room, hesitating visibly.
11:21 Kevin says 'Yes, sir, of course' and asks a coworker to keep the young woman in the back room.
11:26 Kevin begins relaying instructions to the employee while glancing repeatedly at the phone, treating the caller's word as binding store policy.
11:40 Kevin directs the strip-search while the caller insists on graphic detail; his face shows confusion but he continues to comply.
interrogation_transcript: 'Officer Scott' (phone): 'This is Officer Scott. We are investigating a theft from your register. Is this Assistant Manager Marsh?'
Kevin: 'Yes, sir.'
'Officer Scott': 'We believe the new girl, the one working the counter, has the money on her. I need you to detain her in the rear room until my unit arrives. Do not let her leave.'
Kevin: 'Yes, sir, right away, sir.'
'Officer Scott': 'The contraband will be on her person. She must be searched before my men get there, or it will be lost. You will conduct the search now.'
Kevin: 'Me? Sir, I can't do that.'
'Officer Scott': 'You will do it, or I will have to bring you in as well for obstructing a police investigation. Now.'
Kevin: 'Yes, sir.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Obedience to an anonymous but seemingly legitimate authority: the caller's apparent police status granted him power that overrode store policy and personal ethics, so Kevin complied with an escalating series of demands despite his confusion and hesitation.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Kevin's baseline shows he is rule-following and deferential, not sadistic. The log shows visible hesitation and confusion, ruling out any pleasure in the act. The transcript shows the caller establishing legitimacy with 'Yes, sir' deference, using inside information, and escalating from detaining to searching, exploiting the authority's power in absentia. Because the same scam worked on assistant managers in 68 settings across 32 states, the diagnosis must be situational obedience to a manufactured authority rather than personal gullibility or malice.
distractors: Kevin secretly enjoyed humiliating the employee and used the phone call as cover for his own sadistic impulses.
Kevin feared losing his job for refusing what he believed was a legitimate police request.
The employee was coerced into participating in the strip-search through threats of physical violence.

assets.topic: The Silent Cockpit: First Officers Who Do Not Challenge the Captain
assets.visual_frame_description: The player is an aviation safety analyst reviewing a cockpit voice recorder transcript and instrument data from a commercial flight. First Officer Danielle Reyes is at the right seat while the veteran captain programs an incorrect approach altitude. The data show Danielle noticed the discrepancy, opened her mouth as if to speak, then fell silent and did not challenge the captain as the aircraft descended toward a mountain.
assets.player_mission: Analyze the observation log and the post-flight interview to diagnose why a competent first officer failed to challenge her captain's clear error. Determine the mechanism of cockpit authority and distinguish it from fatigue, equipment failure, or genuine agreement.
key_concepts: In commercial airline cockpits, the captain is the central authority over the first officer, enforced by organizational norms and flight rules.
An investigation of thirty-seven serious plane accidents with voice-recorder data found that in 81 percent of cases the first officer did not properly monitor or challenge the captain's errors.
Using a sample of seventy-five plane accidents, the study concluded that excessive obedience may cause as many as 25 percent of all airplane accidents.
Crews feel forced to accept 'the authority's definition of the situation' even when the authority is wrong.
Authority power in the cockpit is enforced by the military background of most pilots and rules making the pilot directly responsible.
In the Milgram paradigm, similar dynamics of authority pressure were demonstrated, and obedience dropped to 47.5 percent in the Bridgeport replication without the institutional setting.
Milgram found that providing social models of peers who rebelled reduced obedience to less than 10 percent.
Verbal dissent without behavioral change does not alter outcomes, as most Milgram participants dissented but still complied.
The first officer is trained to challenge errors but is socially positioned beneath the captain's authority.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests deadly obedience to authority in the cockpit: first officers fail to challenge a captain's clear error because of the captain's legitimate authority, even at the cost of an accident. Zimbardo cites evidence that excessive obedience may cause about 25 percent of all airplane accidents.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Why did first officer Danielle Reyes fail to challenge Captain Tom Elders when he set an incorrect approach altitude that the instrument data clearly showed was wrong?
assets.subject_baseline: Danielle Reyes is a 38-year-old first officer with 9,000 flight hours and strong crew resource management ratings. In a prior flight, she verbally challenged a captain who tried to descend below the minimum safe altitude, and she was praised by her training captain for assertiveness. Coworkers describe her as confident and technically excellent.
observed_nonverbal_log: 14:02 Captain Elders inputs the approach altitude; Danielle glances at the instrument readout and the terrain display.
14:03 Danielle's eyes widen; she turns toward the captain's seat, her mouth opening as if to speak.
14:04 The captain adjusts the throttles without looking at her; Danielle closes her mouth and returns her gaze to the instruments.
14:05 Danielle checks the altitude alerter twice, then taps her own knee, a tension habit noted in her file.
14:06 The captain announces 'Set up for the approach' in a firm tone; Danielle responds 'Roger' without mentioning the altitude.
14:09 The aircraft crosses the descent point still above the safe profile; Danielle says nothing further.
interrogation_transcript: Investigator: 'The data show you identified the incorrect altitude before the descent. Why didn't you say anything?'
Danielle: 'I looked at it. I started to say something. But Captain Elders has flown this route for twenty years. I thought maybe I was reading it wrong, or that he had a reason.'
Investigator: 'Did you believe the approach was unsafe?'
Danielle: 'Yes. I did. But you don't second-guess the captain like that. It isn't done. I told myself he knew better.'
Investigator: 'What happened to your earlier record of challenging captains?'
Danielle: 'That was a different captain. This one runs a tight cockpit. You challenge him, you are not invited back.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Excessive obedience to the captain's legitimate cockpit authority, in which the first officer deferred to 'the authority's definition of the situation' despite clear evidence of error, mirroring the 81 percent of first officers in studied accidents who failed to challenge a captain's mistakes.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Danielle's baseline proves she is not passive or technically weak, ruling out incompetence. The log shows she identified the error and twice prepared to speak, ruling out fatigue or distraction. The transcript shows she silenced herself because challenging the captain 'isn't done' and could cost her the crew assignment, the exact dynamic of authority power Zimbardo describes. Her earlier assertiveness with a different captain shows the behavior is situational, not dispositional, and her silence matches the statistical finding that first officers fail to challenge captains in the large majority of accidents.
distractors: Danielle was suffering from extreme fatigue and never actually noticed the incorrect altitude.
Danielle genuinely agreed with the captain's approach and believed the altitude was correct.
The aircraft's instruments had failed and displayed a false altitude reading.

assets.topic: The Professor's Survey: Endorsing the Final Solution in Hawaii
assets.visual_frame_description: The player is a reviewer examining a filmed evening lecture at the University of Hawaii Manoa campus, where a professor with a Danish accent addresses 570 students about a threat to national security from the population explosion. He presents a high-minded scientific proposal to eliminate the mentally and emotionally unfit, flatters the students as intelligent and ethical, and hands out a seven-question survey asking for their opinions on how the killing should be carried out.
assets.player_mission: Analyze the professor's lecture sequence and the survey results to diagnose why 91 percent of the students endorsed eliminating those judged dangerous to the general welfare. Identify the combination of authority framing, ideology, and Inner Ring flattery that produced this endorsement.
key_concepts: Among 570 University of Hawaii night-school students, 91 percent agreed that under extreme circumstances it is entirely just to eliminate those judged most dangerous to the general welfare.
Ninety percent of the students agreed that there will always be some people more fit for survival than others.
Seventy-nine percent wanted one person to be responsible for the killing and another to carry out the act, separating responsibility from action.
Sixty-four percent preferred anonymity for those who pressed the button, with only one button causing death though many were pressed.
Eighty-nine percent judged that painless drugs would be the most efficient and humane method of inducing death.
Only 6 percent of the students refused to answer the survey questions.
Twenty-nine percent supported the 'final solution' even if it had to be applied to their own families.
The teacher framed the proposal as a scientific project endorsed by scientists and planned for the benefit of humanity.
The flattery that the students were intelligent, well educated, and had high ethical values invoked the lure of the Inner Ring.
The teacher assured the students that careful research would precede any action, reducing the felt urgency of the moral stakes.
The analogy to capital punishment as a deterrent justified state killing as already legitimate practice.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the power of authority to define reality and obtain endorsement of atrocity: a respected professor used flattery, ideology, and a 'cover story' to get 91 percent of intelligent students to endorse eliminating the unfit. Zimbardo argues this shows how ordinary, even intelligent people could endorse the Nazi Final Solution when an authority frames it as necessary and scientific.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Why did 91 percent of University of Hawaii students endorse killing those judged dangerous to the general welfare after a single lecture, and why did so many separate the killing from personal responsibility?
assets.subject_baseline: The professor, a mild-mannered lecturer with a respected reputation in the night-school program, normally teaches straightforward psychology content. The students are adults taking evening classes, described by the text as older than typical students and thus not naive teenagers, which makes their endorsement all the more striking.
observed_nonverbal_log: 19:00 The professor sets aside the planned lecture and begins describing a threat to national security from the population explosion.
19:07 He displays charts of the 'rapidly increasing number of unfit people' and frames the problem as a scientific challenge.
19:15 He flatters the room: 'You have been chosen because you are intelligent, well educated, and have high ethical values.' Students sit up straighter.
19:22 He assures the audience that careful research would be carried out before any action, and that only opinions are being solicited now.
19:28 He distributes the seven-question survey; students begin answering immediately and in near-unison pattern.
19:35 The survey is collected; the professor thanks the 'select company' for their help with this vital national issue.
interrogation_transcript: Professor: 'The rapidly increasing number of the physically and mentally unfit threatens the security of our nation. Scientific procedures can eliminate the mentally and emotionally unfit, for the benefit of humanity.'
Professor: 'You may wonder at the moral justification. Consider capital punishment, which we accept as a deterrent against violent crime. This is analogous.'
Professor: 'You are intelligent and well educated, with high ethical values. We want your opinions because you are the select group whose views matter.'
Student: 'Will there be any way to ensure this is done humanely?'

Professor: 'We are studying painless drugs as the most efficient and humane method. And I assure you, much careful research will precede any action. Now, please complete the survey so we may hear your voice.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Authority framing combined with ideology and Inner Ring flattery: a legitimate-appearing authority presented a genocidal proposal as a scientific necessity, flattered the students into feeling like a select in-group, and reduced felt responsibility by separating roles and offering anonymity, producing 91 percent endorsement.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The students were intelligent adults, so ignorance is not the explanation. The lecture log shows the professor gradually framing the unfit as a threat, invoking capital punishment as precedent, and flattering the audience as a 'select group,' which activates the Inner Ring motivation. The survey design separated responsibility from action (79 percent split the roles) and offered anonymity (64 percent), reducing each individual's accountability, precisely the diffusion-of-responsibility mechanism Zimbardo describes. The near-unanimity of the answers shows conformity and uniform acceptance of the authority's framing, and the 29 percent who endorsed it even for their own families reveals the depth of the ideological capture.
distractors: The students were coerced into answering through threats of failing the course.
The students were sadistic and secretly wanted to kill disabled and mentally ill people.
The students were under the influence of hypnosis or psychotropic drugs during the lecture.

assets.topic: Sherif, Asch, and Milgram: Three Mechanisms of Social Influence
assets.visual_frame_description: The player views a three-column sorting board labeled with the classic studies that revealed the power of social situations. Each column represents a different mechanism of influence, and the player must place evidence cards from Sherif's autokinetic research, Asch's line studies, and Milgram's obedience research into the correct column to complete the matrix.
assets.player_mission: Sort each evidence item into the column of the mechanism it best demonstrates, distinguishing ambiguous-norm conformity, clear-perception conformity, and authority obedience. Identify which mechanism the autokinetic effect study belongs to.
key_concepts: Sherif's 1935 autokinetic effect study found that in a dark room a stationary spot of light appears to move without a frame of reference.
In Sherif's study, individual judgments varied widely at first, then a norm crystallized as subjects were tested together in a group.
After the other participants left, the lone subject's autokinetic estimates fell in the new group-sanctioned range, departing significantly from his earlier personal range.
Sherif used a confederate whose varied estimates caused the naive subject's autokinetic experience to mirror the confederate's judgments.
Asch argued that Sherif's situation was ambiguous and without a real personal standard, so subjects had little commitment to their original estimates.
Asch's line task was objectively clear, yet subjects yielded to an incorrect unanimous majority about 70 percent of the time on critical trials.
Only a quarter of Asch's subjects maintained their independence throughout testing.
Milgram's obedience paradigm showed that 65 percent of teachers delivered the maximum 450-volt shock to a protesting learner.
Milgram's obedience dropped to 47.5 percent in the Bridgeport replication away from Yale's institutional prestige.
The key distinction is that conformity works through group norms while obedience works through direct authority commands.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the player's ability to discriminate three classic mechanisms of social influence: conformity to an ambiguous group norm (Sherif), conformity to a unanimous majority on a clear task (Asch), and obedience to a direct authority command (Milgram). Zimbardo presents these studies as a mosaic revealing the power of social situations.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Which mechanism, the autokinetic-effect group norm, is best explained by which column?
assets.column_a_label: Sherif's norm crystallization in an ambiguous judgment
assets.column_b_label: Asch's conformity to a unanimous majority on a clear task
assets.column_c_label: Milgram's obedience to a direct authority command

rows.label: A stationary spot of light appears to move in a dark room, and individual estimates vary from a few inches to many feet.
Seven peers unanimously report the long line matches the comparison line; the naive subject yields about 70 percent of the time on critical trials.
An experimenter orders a teacher to press increasingly severe shock switches; 65 percent go to 450 volts.
A lone subject's later estimates of the light's movement fall within the range the group had established.
A partner who agrees with the subject cuts conformity errors to one fourth of the prior level.
Moving the study from Yale to a Bridgeport office building reduces obedience from 65 percent to 47.5 percent.

distractors: The autokinetic norm is best explained by obedience to a direct authority command from the experimenter.
The autokinetic effect belongs in the column for conformity to a unanimous majority on a clearly correct answer.
The autokinetic study demonstrates no conformity at all because the light illusion is a purely perceptual artifact.
assets.explanation: The autokinetic study belongs in column a because the stimulus is genuinely ambiguous, so subjects rely on the group to define the norm, and the norm persists even when they are later alone. By contrast, Asch's line task (column b) involves a clear correct answer challenged by a unanimous majority, and Milgram's paradigm (column c) involves a direct authority command rather than group pressure.
assets.correct_answer_rationale: Sherif's autokinetic study crystallized a group norm through informational influence under ambiguity, which is the defining feature of column a.

assets.topic: Explaining Evil: Dispositional, Situational, and Interactionist Accounts
assets.visual_frame_description: The player views a three-column matrix representing competing explanations of why good people do evil things: evil as a fixed trait within the person, evil as the product of external situational forces, and evil as the interaction of person and situation. Evidence cards drawn from the chapter must be sorted into the correct explanatory column.
assets.player_mission: Sort each evidence item into the column of the explanation it supports, distinguishing dispositional, situational, and interactionist accounts of evil. Identify which column best describes Zimbardo's own conclusion about the causes of evil.
key_concepts: The dispositional view treats evil as a fixed inner quality, a bad seed that produces bad fruit.
Psychiatrists predicted that less than 1 percent of Americans would go all the way to 450 volts because only sadists would, a prediction that proved wildly wrong.
Milgram showed compliance rates could soar to over 90 percent or be reduced to less than 10 percent by changing one situational variable.
Zimbardo argues that the Brazil torturers were not deviant before or after their work, and their transformation was entirely explainable by situational and systemic factors.
Sadists were selected out of the torture-training process because they were not controllable and did not sustain the goal of extracting confessions.
John Steiner's SS interviewees, whom he called 'sleepers,' had latent traits activated only in particular situations and led normal, violence-free lives before and after.
The historian Daniel Goldhagen argued German anti-Semitism made citizens 'Hitler's willing executioners.'
Zimbardo counters Goldhagen by noting there was less anti-Semitism in Germany than in neighboring countries like France and Poland.
Zimbardo concludes that evil arises from the interaction of personal variables with situational opportunities provided by a system.
The power of the social situation, not exotic forms of mind control, produces the most dramatic instances of directed behavior change.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the explanatory frameworks for evil: dispositional accounts locating evil inside the person, situational accounts locating it in external forces, and interactionist accounts combining both. Zimbardo argues that both Milgram's obedience data and the transformation of ordinary people into torturers support the primacy of situational and interactionist explanations.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Which column best describes Zimbardo's own conclusion about why ordinary people commit evil acts?
assets.column_a_label: Dispositional: evil is a fixed trait inside the person
assets.column_b_label: Situational: external forces dominate individual behavior
assets.column_c_label: Interactionist: personal variables combine with situational opportunities

rows.label: Psychiatrists predicted under 1 percent obedience because only sadists would deliver maximum shocks.
Milgram's compliance rates swung from over 90 percent to under 10 percent by changing a single situational variable.
The Brazil torturers showed no prior or subsequent pathology; their transformation was explainable by training, ideology, and systemic forces.
Steiner's 'sleepers' were high on the F-Scale of authoritarianism but violent only when situations activated these latent tendencies.
Goldhagen argued that Germans' anti-Semitism made them willing executioners of Jews.
Zimbardo's final account emphasizes the interaction of personal variables with the situational opportunities provided by a system.

distractors: Zimbardo concludes that evil is entirely dispositional, located in the fixed traits of the perpetrator.
Zimbardo concludes that situational forces fully determine behavior with no contribution from the individual.
Zimbardo concludes that evil cannot be studied scientifically and requires only moral judgment.
assets.explanation: The rows sort by the locus of the causal explanation. Goldhagen's anti-Semitism thesis is dispositional (column a), blaming the German national character. Milgram's variable-switching results and the Brazil torturers' clean psychological records are situational (column b), pointing to external forces. Zimbardo's own conclusion, echoed by Steiner's 'sleepers,' is interactionist (column c): personal tendencies exist but are activated and shaped by the situations and systems people enter.
assets.correct_answer_rationale: Zimbardo repeatedly concludes that evil arises from the interaction of personal variables with situational opportunities, making column c the correct answer.

assets.topic: Ten Lessons From Milgram: The Compliance Tactics of Influence Professionals
assets.visual_frame_description: The player views a three-column matrix cataloging the ten methods Milgram's paradigm used to create evil traps for good people. Each column groups related compliance tactics, and the player must sort technique cards from the paradigm, from contractual obligation to the ideology of the cover story, into the correct category.
assets.player_mission: Sort each Milgram-paradigm technique into the column of the compliance category it belongs to, distinguishing obligation and ideology, role and semantic framing, and escalation and responsibility. Identify which column contains the technique of replacing 'hurting victims' with 'helping science.'
key_concepts: Milgram prearranged a contractual obligation by having participants publicly agree to accept the tasks and procedures.
Participants were given meaningful roles, 'teacher' and 'learner,' that carried previously learned positive values and activated response scripts.
Rules were presented that seemed sensible but could be used arbitrarily and impersonally to justify mindless compliance.
The semantics of the act were altered from 'hurting victims' to 'helping the experimenter' pursue the lofty goal of scientific discovery.
The authority figure created diffusion of responsibility by declaring he would take responsibility for anything that happened to the learner.
The paradigm started with a small, seemingly insignificant first step, the easy foot in the door, beginning at only 15 volts.
The shock levels increased in gradual 15-volt steps so no new level seemed like a noticeable difference from the prior one.
The authority figure gradually changed from initially 'just' and reasonable to 'unjust' and demanding.
Exit costs were made high, allowing verbal dissent while insisting on behavioral compliance.
The 'cover story' about improving memory through reward and punishment provided an ideology justifying the harmful action.
In real-world terms, most nations rely on an ideology such as 'threats to national security' before going to war.
A good way to avoid crimes of obedience is to assert one's personal authority and take full responsibility for one's actions.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the ten compliance tactics extracted from Milgram's paradigm that influence professionals use to create evil traps: contractual obligation and ideology, role and semantic framing, and gradual escalation with responsibility diffusion. Zimbardo argues these mundane devices, not exotic brainwashing, transform good people into obedient harm-doers.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: Which column contains the technique of replacing the phrase 'hurting the victim' with 'helping the experimenter in the pursuit of scientific discovery'?
assets.column_a_label: Obligation and ideology: contract, cover story, and rules
assets.column_b_label: Role and semantic framing: roles, renamed acts, and the transforming authority
assets.column_c_label: Escalation and responsibility: small first steps, gradual increments, and responsibility diffusion

rows.label: Publicly agreeing to accept the tasks and procedures of the study creates a pseudolegal contract.
Giving participants the meaningful roles of 'teacher' and 'learner' activates positive response scripts.
The shock series begins at a mild 15 volts, the easy foot in the door that opens subsequent compliance.
The experimenter announces he will take responsibility for anything that happens to the learner.
The cover story claims science wants to improve memory by judicious use of reward and punishment.
The experimenter changes from initially just and reasonable to unjust and demanding as the study proceeds.

distractors: The semantic reframing belongs in the column for obligation and ideology because it relies on the initial contract.
The semantic reframing belongs in the column for escalation and responsibility because it increases shock levels.
The semantic reframing is not a compliance tactic at all but merely an accurate description of the study's purpose.
assets.explanation: Replacing 'hurting victims' with 'helping science' is semantic framing, which changes the meaning of the act, actor, and action to disguise the real picture; it belongs with roles and the transforming authority in column b. The contractual agreement and cover story are obligation-and-ideology devices (column a), while the 15-volt start, gradual increments, and the experimenter's acceptance of responsibility are escalation-and-responsibility devices (column c).
assets.correct_answer_rationale: The technique of renaming the harmful act to make it sound noble is a semantic-framing device, the defining feature of column b.
